blocks.text: It has been observed experimentally that when a conductor moves across a magnetic field, an electromotive force (emf) is induced between its ends. The induced emf in the moving conductor is similar to that of a battery: if the ends of the conductor are connected by a wire to form a closed circuit, a current flows through it.

blocks.title: Motional emf
blocks.text: The emf induced by the motion of a conductor across a magnetic field is called motional emf.

Consider the experiment of Fig. 10.13. A conducting rod of length L is placed on two parallel metal rails separated by a distance L. A galvanometer is connected between the ends c and d of the rails, forming a complete conducting loop abcda. A uniform magnetic field B is directed into the page. Initially, when the rod is stationary, the galvanometer indicates no current. If the rod is pulled to the right with constant velocity v, the galvanometer indicates a current flowing through the loop. Obviously the current is induced by the motion of the rod across the magnetic field; the moving rod acts as a source of emf epsilon = Vb - Va = delta V.

blocks.alt: Two horizontal rails, top end c and bottom end d, are joined on the left through a galvanometer. A copper rod ab (b at the top, a at the bottom) lies across them; the green region between has crosses for B into the paper. A charge q in the rod moves right with velocity v. Current arrows I point left along the top rail, down beside the galvanometer and right along the bottom rail. L marks the rail spacing.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.13: Motional emf: a rod moved with velocity v along rails in a magnetic field into the paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.13).

blocks.text: When the rod moves, a charge q within it also moves with the same velocity v in the field B and experiences the force F = q v x B (Eq. 10.13), of magnitude qvB sin theta. Since the angle between v and B is 90 degrees, F = qvB ... (10.16). By the right-hand rule the force on q is directed from a to b along the rod, so charges migrate to the top end b, while there is a deficiency of charge at the bottom end a. This redistribution creates an electrostatic field E directed from b to a, and an electrostatic force qE on the charge from b to a. The system quickly reaches an equilibrium in which these two forces are balanced: qE = qvB, or E = vB ... (10.17).

In this equilibrium the motional emf equals the potential difference delta V = Vb - Va between the ends of the rod. The electric field is the negative of the potential gradient, E = -delta V/L ... (10.18), giving delta V = -LE = -(LvB) and epsilon = delta V = -LvB ... (10.19); its magnitude is vBL. If the angle between v and B is theta, epsilon = -vBL sin theta ... (10.20). Because of the induced emf, positive charges flow along the path abcda, so the induced current is anticlockwise in the diagram. As the current flows, the charge at the top decreases, reducing the electric field while the magnetic force stays the same; this imbalance favours the magnetic force, so as charges reach the end a through the circuit they are carried back to the top end b by the magnetic force, and the current continues to flow.

The motional emf induced in a rod moving perpendicular to a magnetic field is epsilon = -vBL. The motional emf, as well as other induced emfs, can be described in terms of magnetic flux. Consider the experiment of Fig. 10.14: the rod moves from position 1 to position 2 in a small time delta t, travelling a distance delta x = x2 - x1. Since it moves with constant velocity, v = delta x/delta t ... (10.21). Putting this in Eq. 10.19, epsilon = -vBL = -(delta x/delta t) BL ... (10.22). As the rod moves through delta x, the area of the loop increases by delta A = delta x L, which increases the flux through the loop by delta phi = (delta A) B. Putting (delta x L) B = delta phi in Eq. 10.22 gives epsilon = -delta phi/delta t ... (10.23).

blocks.alt: The same rails and galvanometer, with the rod shown dashed at Position 1 and solid at Position 2. Below, x1 runs from the galvanometer end to Position 1, delta x from Position 1 to Position 2, and x2 from the galvanometer end to Position 2. The strip between the positions is marked delta A; L marks the rail spacing; current I points left along the top rail; B is into the paper.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.14: The rod moves from Position 1 to Position 2 through delta x, increasing the loop area by delta A (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.14).

blocks.text: Equation (10.20) shows that if the magnetic flux through a single loop is changing, the negative of the rate of change of flux equals the emf induced in the loop. For a coil of N loops the induced emf becomes N times: epsilon = -N delta phi/delta t ... (10.24). Although this was derived from motional emf, it is true in general. This conclusion was first reached by Faraday, so it is known as Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book writes Equation (10.20) here, but Eq. 10.20 is epsilon = -vBL sin theta. The flux equation epsilon = -delta phi/delta t is Eq. 10.23.

blocks.title: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction
blocks.text: The average emf induced in a conducting coil of N loops is equal to the negative of the rate at which the magnetic flux through the coil is changing with time. The minus sign indicates that the direction of the induced emf is such that it opposes the change in flux.

blocks.alt: A copper ring falls straight down through positions 1 to 5. Positions 2 and 4 are at the top and bottom edges of a rectangular region with crosses for a field into the page, and position 3 is inside it. blocks.text: Wireless charging works on the principle of electromagnetic induction (Do You Know). On an induction heater the water in a metal pot boils while that in a glass pot does not, and even the glass top stays cool: the coil beneath carries alternating current that produces a changing flux; the flux linking the pots induces an emf, and current is generated in the metal pot, but no current flows through the glass pan. Why? (For Your Information).
